Coupling Iron Sludge Addition and Intermittent Aeration for
Achieving Simultaneous Methanogenesis, Feammox, and
Denitrification in a Single Reactor Treating Fish Sludge
Qing Xia,⊥Fei Liu,⊥Shengrui Sun, Wenli Huang, Ziwen Zhao, Fei Yang, Zhongfang Lei,
Weiwei Huang,* and Xuesong Yi*
Cite This: Environ. Sci. Technol. 2023, 57, 15065−15075

ABSTRACT: An integrated anaerobic digestion system for the
simultaneous removal of carbon and nitrogen from fish sludge was
developed by coupling iron sludge supplementation with
intermittent aeration. In terms of nitrogen removal, Fe(III) in
iron sludge could trigger Feammox reactions and intermittent
aeration could drive the Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle to sustain continuous
ammonia removal. Mass balance analysis suggested that nitrate was
the main product of Feammox, which was subsequently removed
through heterotrophic denitrification. In terms of carbon removal,
the Fe(III)-induced dissimilatory iron reduction (DIR) process
significantly promoted fish sludge hydrolysis and provided more
simple organics for methanogens and denitrifiers, but aeration
showed a negative impact on methanogenesis. To promote
nitrogen removal and avoid serious methanogenesis inhibition,
different aeration intensities were studied. Results showed that compared with the control without aeration or iron sludge addition,
aeration for 5 min every 3 days (150 mL/min) contributed to a 29.0% lower NH4
+-N concentration and a 12.1% lower total
chemical oxygen demand level on day 28, and the decline in methane yield was acceptable (only 13.5% lower). Simultaneous
methanogenesis, Feammox, and denitrification in a single reactor treating fish sludge were achieved, which provides a simple and
low-cost strategy for the treatment of organic wastewater.
KEYWORDS: fish sludge, nitrogen removal, carbon removal, CH4 recovery, Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle, metagenomic analysis
1. INTRODUCTION
Huge amounts of fish sludge, consisting of fecal solids and
undigested feed, are generated each year from the freshwater
aquaculture industry globally and require proper treatment and
utilization. Anaerobic digestion (AD) is an environmentally
friendly process that converts organic matter into combustible
methane (CH4), and has long been practiced for the treatment
of fish sludge.1 However, the digestates containing high levels
of ammonia require further treatment before discharge. The
normal practice is to set up biological nitrogen (N) removal
units after AD, which not only complicates the treatment
procedure but also increases the energy consumption, land use,
and construction cost.2,3 Therefore, it is necessary to develop
integrated anaerobic treatment systems for the simultaneous
removal of carbon (C) and N.
In recent years, researchers have successfully coupled
methanogenesis and denitrification in a single reactor,
achieving simultaneous removal of organic C and nitrate/
nitrite.4,5 The small molecular organic substances produced
from the fermentation process can provide carbon sources for
the denitrifiers, and the alkalinity generated during the
denitrification reactions can create a more stable environment
for the methanogens.4,5 Despite the merits of simultaneous
methanogenesis and the denitrification process, the organic N
rich in fish sludge is mainly decomposed to ammonia during
AD, which cannot be directly utilized by denitrifiers. The
conventional ammonia oxidation and nitrite oxidation
processes generally function at a dissolved oxygen (DO)
concentration no less than 0.4 and 3.0 mg/L, respectively,6
which are difficult to occur in AD reactors. Therefore, finding
effective strategies to convert ammonium-nitrogen (NH4
+-N)
into nitrite-nitrogen (NO2
−-N) or nitrate-nitrogen (NO3
−-N)
under anaerobic environments is the key to simultaneously

achieving N removal and CH4 recovery in a single reactor
treating fish sludge.
Anaerobic ammonium oxidation coupling with Fe(III)
reduction (Feammox) has recently been discovered as a new
pathway for N removal.7−9 During this process, Fe(III) was
utilized as the electron acceptor to oxidize NH4
+-N into
nitrogen gas (N2), NO2
−-N, or NO3
−-N. Theoretically, the
formed NOx
−can be further utilized by heterotrophic
denitrifiers in the presence of an adequate amount of organic
C.10 Therefore, the implementation of Feammox in AD
reactors is expected to advance the conversion of NH4
+-N into
N2 by coupling with denitrification. Iron-reducing bacteria
(IRBs) are identified as the key mediators of Feammox
process, and various Fe(III) compounds including Fe2O3,
Fe(OH)3, FeCl3, pyrite, magnetite, and goethite have been
proven to be effective for enriching IRBs and triggering
Feammox reactions.10,11 Iron sludge that mainly consists of
Fe(OH)3 is a type of waste generated from Fenton reactions
(for advanced treatment of the aquaculture effluent) or iron-
salt-based flocculation (for solid−liquid separation). The good
availability, relatively high solubility, large specific surface area,
high microbial accessibility, and low crystallinity of iron sludge
make it an ideal Fe(III) source. It is noteworthy that the
Feammox efficiency is positively correlated with the microbial
reducible Fe(III) content.11 To sustain successive Feammox
reactions for NH4
+-N removal from N-rich fish sludge, a large
amount of exogenous Fe(III) is needed, which is impractical
from an economical or environmental point of view. What is
more, the formed Fe(II) could attach to the surface of Fe(III)
compounds, changing their thermodynamic properties and
accelerating their transformation into more crystalline
minerals,12 which further decreases the microbial reducible
Fe(III). To increase the utilization efficiency of Fe(III), it is
important to find effective strategies to convert Fe(II) into
Fe(III) in a timely manner and reutilize it in the next round of
Feammox.
Oxygen (O2) is a cheap, readily available, and effective
oxidant. The oxidation of Fe(II) into Fe(III) can occur at a
very low DO level of less than 0.02 mg/L,13 which is much
lower than that of conventional nitrification process. A low
level of DO would not seriously inhibit the AD process.
Instead, the dosing of a small amount of air or O2 (DO range
of 0.1−1.0 mg/L) into the AD system could effectively
enhance the degradation of organics through promoting the
growth and metabolisms of facultative bacteria.14 To achieve
effective N removal from the AD reactor without significantly
deteriorating the methanogenesis performance, the aeration
intensity needs to be optimized. Several studies have employed
Feammox-based reactors for the simultaneous removal of
ammonia and organics by creating a DO fluctuation environ-
ment. Yang et al. reported that by periodically increasing the
DO to 0.4 mg/L through intermittent aeration, Fe(III) was
regenerated and involved in the next run of Feammox and
dissimilatory iron reduction (DIR).15 After 90 days of reaction,
the overall removal efficiencies of total nitrogen (TN) and total
chemical oxygen demand (TCOD) were 98.5 and 43.2%,
respectively. Ma et al. observed the Fe(III)/Fe(II) redox cycle
in a Feammox-based up-flow anaerobic reactor using limonite
as the filter medium.16 The initial DO was 0.58 mg/L, which
gradually decreased as the water flowed upward. Results
showed that more than 55.0% of influent TCOD was removed
in the lower layer of the reactor, while 60.2% of NH4
+-N was
removed in the middle layer. These previous studies are mainly
focused on the removal of N and C; little attention was paid to
the CH4 recovery efficiency or the syntrophic relationship
between Feammox and denitrification. To our acknowledg-
ment, the feasibility of coupling methanogenesis, Feammox,
and denitrification in a single reactor has not been studied yet.
The microbial interactions in the integrated system and the
effect of aeration intensity on the conversion of C and N
remain to be explored.
In this study, a novel simultaneous methanogenesis,
Feammox, and denitrification (SMFD) system was developed
for the treatment of fish sludge by coupling iron sludge
addition with intermittent aeration. The performances of CH4
production and N removal at different aeration intensities (5,
10, and 15 min every 3 days at a constant rate of 150 mL/min)
were systematically investigated. Microbial analysis was also
carried out to investigate the microbial community distribu-
tions, diversities, functional traits, and microbial interactions in
the SMFD system.
2. MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1. Materials. The iron sludge used in this study was
prepared through a Fenton process in a 1-L glass beaker at
room temperature. Specifically, 69.5 g of FeSO4·7H2O was
dissolved in 500 mL of deionized water. After complete
dissolution of FeSO4·7H2O, 85 mL of a H2O2 solution (30%
mass fraction) was added. The molar ratio of H2O2 to Fe2+ was
3:1.17 After 2 h of reaction, the system pH was adjusted to 7.0
with NaOH solution (1 mol/L). After precipitation for about
24 h, the liquid was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 10 min. The
collected iron sludge with a moisture content of about 55% was
stored at 4 °C before use.
Fresh fish sludge was collected from a tilapia fish farm
located in Wenchang (China), transferred to the laboratory,
and immediately stored at 4 °C. The seed sludge was taken
from a commercial-scale digester in Baishamen municipal
wastewater treatment plant (Haikou, China), and was mixed
thoroughly with fish sludge and incubated at 35 °C in a lab-
scale batch digester (40-L). During the incubation period, 10 g
of iron sludge was added to the digester on a weekly basis for
the enrichment of IRBs. To guarantee complete decomposition
of the labile organics, the incubation process lasted for 2
months. The mature digestate from this digester was used as
the inoculum in this work. Biogas production from the
inoculum during subsequent experiments was negligible. Basic
characteristics of fish sludge and the inoculum are listed in
Table S1.
2.2. Batch Experiments. In this study, a series of identical
cylindrical glass reactors (188 mm in diameter and 278 mm in
height) was used for the batch AD experiments. As shown in
Figure S1, two types of AD systems were set up, namely, the
aerated system and control system. For the aerated system, air
was intermittently bubbled into the liquid via a gas diffuser at
the bottom of the reactor. Intermittent aeration was achieved
by using an electric timing control switch (Bull, China) and a
12 V DC micro gas pump (Xinweicheng, China). The air flow
rate was maintained at a constant level of 150 mL/min. Liquid
samples were taken periodically from the aerated reactors for
DO analysis during one aeration cycle. The digesters were
sealed with silicon stoppers, and the biogas produced from
each reactor was collected in a gas sampling bag for analysis
every day. Before each aeration cycle, the collected biogas was
quantified. After aeration, the air captured by the gas bag was

discharged immediately to minimize the dilution effect of air

Each reactor received 700 g of fish sludge and 300 g of
inoculum (fish sludge to inoculum ratio of 3:1 based on
volatile solids (VS)), and it was diluted with deionized water to
a final volume of 1.5 L. Main characteristics of the mixture are
listed in Table S1. To study the sole effect of iron sludge
addition, 2 experimental groups were set up, namely, the
Fe(III) group with the addition of 10 g of iron sludge and the
control group without iron sludge. To study the effect of
different aeration intensities, 3 experimental groups added with
10 g of iron sludge were aerated for 5, 10, and 15 min every 3
days since day 4 at a constant rate of 150 mL/min, and were
denoted as Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15,
respectively. Each experimental group was prepared in
duplicate. All reactors were flushed with N2 for 20 min prior
to the experiment and were incubated at 35 °C for 28 days.
To evaluate the possible contribution of aeration to NH4
+
conversion/removal, an additional group of AD experiments
was performed with aeration (150 mL/min for 10 min every 3
days) and without Fe(III) addition (AE10). Other exper-
imental conditions were the same as the Fe(III)-AE10 group.
2.3. Analysis Methods. The biogas production volume
was recorded by using a syringe. The biogas compositions were
analyzed using a gas chromatograph (FULI, GC9790Plus)
with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a packed
column. Argon (purity >99.999%) was used as the carrier gas.

propionic acid (HPr), n-butyric acid (n-HBu), and n-valeric acid (n-HVa).

The injector, column, and detector temperatures were set at
80, 50, and 80 °C, respectively.
For the determination of the key process parameters, liquid
samples were taken periodically. The pH values were measured
by using a pH meter (AS600, ASONE, Japan). The DO was
measured by using a DO sensor (ST400D, OHAUS, China).
The TCOD, total solids (TS), VS, and TN were measured at
the beginning and the end of the experiments according to
Standard Methods.18 The organic C and N contents of the
inoculum, fish sludge, and mixture were analyzed by an
elemental analyzer (PerkinElmer 2004 CHN, USA). For
analysis of soluble compounds, liquid samples were centrifuged
at 9000 rpm for 20 min and filtered through a 0.22-μm
membrane. A gas chromatograph (FULI, GC9790Plus)
equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) and a
capillary column (30 m, 0.32 mm I.D., 0.5 μm) was used to
determine the concentrations of volatile fatty acids (VFAs).
The column temperature was increased from 80 to 180 °C at a
rate of 10 °C/min, and the temperatures of the injector and
detector were 250 and 280 °C, respectively. Argon gas (purity
>99.999%) was applied as the carrier gas. The filtrate was
analyzed for soluble polysaccharides (PS), proteins (PN), and
soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD) as described
previously.19 NO2
−-N, NO3
−-N, and NH4
+-N were determined
according to standard methods.18 Fe(II) concentration was
analyzed according to the procedure described by Ding et al.20
Briefly, 1 mL of the slurry was immediately added to 5 mL of
HCl solution (1 mol/L) in a sealed glass tube. The tube was
shaken for 24 h and subsequently centrifuged at 9000 rpm for
20 min. The supernatant was then measured for ferric iron
concentration according to the standard method.18
2.4. Microbial metagenomic Analysis. At the end of the
experiment, digestates from duplicate reactors were mixed
thoroughly prior to microbial analysis. Samples from all
experimental groups were collected for metagenomic analysis.
The total DNA of each microbial sample was extracted using
the FastDNA SPIN Kit for soil (MP Biochemicals Inc., US).
The DNA extract was fragmented to an average size of about
400 bp using a Covaris M220 (Gene Company Limited,
China). Paired-end library was constructed using NEXTFLEX
Rapid DNA-Seq (Bioo Scientific, US). Paired-end sequencing
was performed on the NovaSeq platform (Illumina, USA) at
Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China).
The data were analyzed on the free online platform of
Majorbio Cloud Platform (www.majorbio.com).
2.5. Statistical Analyses. One-way analysis of variance
was conducted to compare the experimental data using SPSS
22.0 (US), and statistical significance was accepted at p < 0.05.
3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
3.1. Methane Production and Organic Removal. The
CH4 production efficiency is a key indicator for evaluating the
performance of AD. The CH4 potentials of fish sludge depend
highly upon the type of fish, feed components, and feeding
pattern. Mirzoyan et al. reported an accumulative CH4 yield of
77.5 mL/g-VSfed from up-flow anaerobic sludge blanket
(UASB) reactors treating striped bass sludge.21 Gebauer et
al. obtained a higher CH4 yield of 123.6−266.3 mL/g-VSfed
from the fish sludge of Atlantic salmon in a continuous stirred
tank reactor (CSTR) at 35 °C.22 As shown in Figure 1a, the
accumulative CH4 yields in all reactors rose rapidly on day 0
and flattened out after day 20, suggesting that the labile
substances were quickly consumed within a short period of 20
days. After 28 days of AD, the accumulative CH4 yield of the
control, Fe(III), Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15
groups reached 71.9, 81.9, 62.2, 43.4, and 37.0 mL/g-VSfed,
respectively. The CH4 yields obtained in this work were
comparable to those in the literature. The CH4 yield of the
Fe(III) group was 13.9% higher (p < 0.05) than that of the
control group, indicating the effectiveness of iron sludge in
improving the methanogenesis performance. The phenomenon
was consistent with the results obtained by Wang et al., who
attained an improved CH4 yield by 12.6−21.0% during AD of
waste-activated sludge (WAS) with the addition of 2 to 8 g/L
of Fenton sludge.23 The poorly crystalline Fe(III) hydroxides
in iron sludge could enrich IRBs that are capable of
metabolizing complex organic substrates through the DIR
process, which promoted the hydrolysis of organic particulates
into smaller molecular substances to benefit methanogenesis.23
In contrast to Fe(III) addition only, aeration showed a
negative effect on AD of fish sludge. Compared with the
control group, a slightly lower level of CH4 yield by 13.5% was
attained in the Fe(III)-AE5 group, and significantly lower
levels of CH4 yield by 39.6 and 48.5% were observed in the
Fe(III)-AE10 and Fe(III)-AE15 groups, respectively. The
results were expected since a high O2 level is known to be
toxic to methanogens.24
The TCOD concentrations before and after the AD
experiments are shown in Figure 1b. The initial TCOD
concentration of the sludge was 22166.5 mg/L, the remaining
concentrations of which after AD were determined to be
13610.2, 12657.1, 11969.9, 11327.1, and 10972.4 mg/L in the
control, Fe(III), Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15
groups, respectively. The corresponding TCOD removal
efficiencies were calculated to be 38.6% for the control,
42.9% for Fe(III), 46.0% for Fe(III)-AE5, 48.9% for Fe(III)-
AE10, and 50.5% for Fe(III)-AE15, respectively. Apparently,
the supplementation of iron sludge significantly increased the
TCOD removal efficiencies (p < 0.05). As discussed above, the
DIR process induced by Fe(III) hydroxides might partially
explain the greater organic degradation efficiencies in the
Fe(III)-supplemented digesters. It was noticeable that in spite
of the significantly lower CH4 yield from the three aerated
groups, the TCOD removal efficiencies of the Fe(III)-AE5,
Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15 groups were 19.2, 26.7, and
30.8% greater than the control group, respectively. The organic
removal efficiencies were positively correlated with aeration
time, which could be supported by the CO2 production result
displayed in Figure S2. As shown, the accumulative CO2 yield
increased significantly with the aeration time, and these might
be explained by the following reasons: (1) the injected O2
could support the growth and metabolisms of facultative
organisms, which effectively enhanced the degradation of
organics14; (2) a certain proportion of the regenerated Fe(III)
via O2 oxidation could engage in the DIR reactions; and (3)
the Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle could drive the Feammox process to
generate more NOx
−, which was further converted into N2 via
heterotrophic denitrification, resulting in the consumption of
greater amounts of organics.
Figure 1c demonstrates the variations of the sCOD with
time. The sCOD concentrations in different reactors varied
similarly, which increased rapidly from the beginning of the
experiment and hit the top on day 4, mainly caused by the
hydrolysis of macromolecular substances. In the following
days, the sCOD in all groups gradually decreased to a low level
after day 20, suggesting that most labile substrates were

effectively consumed by the microorganisms. These results
agreed with the cessation of methanogenesis after day 20. The
variations of soluble PS and PN are illustrated in Figure 1d,e,
respectively. Both substances exhibited a decreasing trend with
time, and their concentrations in the four experimental groups
with iron sludge supplementation were significantly lower than
those in the control group (p < 0.05), which might be
explained by the promotion effect of iron sludge on the
degradation of soluble PS and PN into smaller molecular
organics, which facilitated their subsequent utilization by
bacteria (e.g., acetogens, IRBs, heterotrophic denitrifiers, etc.)
or methanogens. As illustrated in Figure 1f, acetic acid (HAc)
and propionic acid (HPr) were the main components of VFAs,
and the trends of VFAs were similar to those of sCOD. The
VFAs in all groups increased rapidly within the first 4 days, and
then, they gradually decreased until the end of the experiment.
Correspondingly, the pH in all groups decreased within the
first 4 days and then gradually increased with the consumption
of VFAs and stabilized after 16 days (Figure S3). On day 4, the
VFA concentration of the Fe(III) group (3061.9 mg/L) was
significantly higher than that of the control group (2710.0 mg/
L) (p < 0.05). This indicated that iron sludge supplementation
had facilitated the production of VFAs at the early stage of AD,
which could be attributed to the enhanced enzymatic activities
involved in hydrolysis and acidification.25 At the end of AD,
the VFA concentration of the Fe(III) group (680.6 mg/L) was
lower than that of the control group (901.2 mg/L) (p < 0.05),
suggesting that iron sludge had accelerated the decomposition
of VFAs via methanogenesis or other pathways at the late stage
of AD. For the aerated reactors, the highest VFA
concentrations were recorded at 2791.6, 2688.0, and 2696.0
mg/L in the Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15
groups on day 4, respectively. These values were quite close to
that of the Fe(III) group on the same day. Apparently, aeration
did not significantly hinder the acidification performance. At
the late stage of AD (days 16−28), the concentrations of VFAs
in the aerated reactors were higher than that of the control
group, especially the Fe(III)-AE10 and Fe(III)-AE15 groups.
This indicated that higher aeration intensities significantly
inhibited the conversion of VFAs to CH4 (Figure 1a).
3.2. Nitrogen Removal. Figure 2a depicts the changes in
NH4
+-N in different groups. During AD of protein-rich fish
sludge, protein is decomposed stepwise into polypeptides,
amino acids, and short-chain organic acids. Ammonia
accumulates gradually with the anaerobic decomposition
process. In the control group, NH4
+-N increased gradually
from an initial value of 143.1 to 309.8 mg/L by the end of AD.
The addition of iron sludge contributed to a lower level of
NH4
+-N in the Fe(III) group (p < 0.05), with a final NH4
+-N
concentration of 241.6 mg/L being recorded at the end of AD,
which was 22.0% lower than that of the control. Apparently,
the supplementation of Fe(III) led to the loss of NH4
+-N
during AD of the fish sludge. The oxidation of NH4
+-N in an
anaerobic environment is quite challenging due to the lack of
appropriate electron acceptors. Anammox process can
effectively oxidize NH4
+-N using NO2
−-N as an electron
acceptor under anaerobic conditions, and the existence of
Fe(III) may improve the activity of Anammox.26However,
autotrophic Anammox bacteria are characterized by their slow
growth rate and susceptibility to high organic contents.27

Anammox bacteria will be inhibited at a C/N ratio above 2.0,28
and they will be seriously suppressed and outcompeted by the
heterotrophic bacteria at C/N > 4.0.29 Complete suppression
of the Anammox process was observed at TCOD concen-
trations above 700 mg/L.30 In this work, the initial C/N ratio
(15.7) and TCOD concentration (22,166.5 mg/L) of the
mixture were much higher than the inhibitory threshold values
of Anammox. Therefore, Anammox reactions were unlikely to
occur during AD of fish sludge, and the loss of NH4
+-N could
be attributed to other Fe(III)-inducing ammonia oxidation
processes like Feammox. Compared with the case of iron
sludge addition only, coupling iron sludge addition with
intermittent aeration further decreased the NH4
+-N concen-
trations in the Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15
groups. This result was expected since continuous Feammox
reactions could be driven by the Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle with O2
as the terminal electron acceptor.15 It should be mentioned
that aeration might also induce ammonia stripping and
nitrification to accelerate NH4
+ loss. To quantify the possible
contributions of stripping and nitrification, an additional set of
AD experiments (AE10 group) were performed, and the
variations of NH4
+-N are displayed in Figure S4. As indicated,
the final NH4
+-N concentration in the AE10 group was 308.7
mg/L, which was very close to that of the control. The result
suggested that neither stripping nor nitrification played an
important role in NH4
+-N removal. The greater NH4
+-N loss
with intermittent aeration was mostly attributable to the
Feammox process driven by the regenerated Fe(III), and this
will be discussed later in Section 3.3. Despite the positive effect
of aeration on promoting the Feammox process, an increased
aeration time from 5 to 15 min did not significantly lower the
system NH4
+-N concentration (p > 0.05). On day 28, the
NH4
+-N concentrations were 220.1, 215.2, and 211.0 mg/L in
the Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15 groups,
respectively. Feammox is an anoxic process, and a low level of
DO favors the reactions.11 Yao et al. observed a quick decline
in the Feammox rate at a DO level above 1.0 mg/L.31 To
assess the possible toxicity of DO to the Feammox bacteria in
the intermittent aerated reactors, the variations of DO during
one aeration cycle on day 4 were tested (Figure S5). After 5,
10, and 15 min of aeration, the DO concentration increased to
0.06, 0.14, and 0.20 mg/L, respectively. When the aeration was
stopped, the DO was quickly consumed by the microorganisms
and became undetectable within 30−60 min. These DO levels
were not expected to significantly suppress the Feammox
process, and the trade-off between oxygen inhibition and
Fe(III) regeneration was clearly not the reason for the
insignificant improvement in NH4
+-N removal efficiency at
higher aeration intensities. From the experimental results in
this work, it was hypothesized that although a sufficient
amount of Fe(III) was a prerequisite for the Feammox process,
the removal of NH4
+-N was restricted by the slow Feammox
reaction rate. In a review by Xia et al., the N removal rates of
nitrification-denitrification, Anammox, and partial denitrifica-
tion-Anammox were calculated to be 21−58, 106−876, and
310−730 N/m3/day, respectively.11 Compared with these N
removal processes, the reaction rate of Feammox is much
slower. Yang et al. reported that it took 90 days to achieve
98.5% of TN removal from a Feammox reactor (initial TN of
1021.5 mg/L),15 and the N removal rate was calculated to be
11.2 g N/m3/day. In this study, the N removal rates in the
Fe(III)-supplemented reactors during days 2−6 were calcu-
lated to be 9.2−12.8 g N/m3/day. To further improve the
Feammox performance, future research efforts should focus on
the acceleration of the reactions by optimizing the operational
parameters or establishing direct interspecies electron transfer
(DIET) by adding electron shuttles.
It is worth noting that the NH4
+-N concentrations in the
four Fe(III)-supplemented digesters showed a trend of rapid
decline since day 20. As discussed above in Section 3.1, a
certain proportion of Fe(III) could engage in the DIR process.
Feammox was not dominant in Fe(III) reduction at high
organic concentrations because it was at a disadvantage when
competing with DIR for electron acceptors.32 Ding et al.
reported that only 2.2% of Fe(III) reduction was directly
attributed to the Feammox process in paddy soils.20 Therefore,
Fe(III) in digesters treating fish sludge preferentially oxidized
organics rather than ammonia. By day 20, most easily
biodegradable organics were consumed, which was evidenced
by the flattening of accumulative CH4 yield and sCOD (Figure
1a,c), and this could explain the rapid decline of NH4
+-N after
day 20 when Feammox started to gain advantages.
Figure 2b illustrates the changes in NO3
−-N. The initial
NO3
−-N concentration in all groups was 18.6 mg/L. In the
control group, NO3
−-N increased to a maximum value of 27.1
mg/L by day 6, followed by a gradual decline until the end of
AD. The slight increase of NO3
−-N during days 0−6 in the
control group might be attributed to Feammox process
induced by the small amount of Fe(III) in the inoculum and
raw fish sludge. In comparison, NO3
−-N concentrations of the
four Fe(III)-supplemented reactors increased from 13.3 to
17.0 to 69.0−74.3 mg/L during days 2−8, which was in
accordance with the decrease of NH4
+-N in these reactors from
180.4 to 188.6 to 130.9−147.5 mg/L during the same period
(Figure 2a). Mass balance analysis indicated that NO3
−-N was
the main product of Feammox in the Fe(III)-supplemented
reactors. After day 8, the NO3
−-N concentrations in the four
reactors dropped quickly to below 3.0 mg/L by day 20 and
leveled off after that, confirming the occurrence of some
biological or biochemical NO3
−-N removal processes like
denitrification or NOx
−-dependent Fe(II) oxidation (NDFO).
Theoretically, the generated NOx
−can be converted into N2
via the NDFO process, but the autotrophic NDFO bacteria did
not have a growth advantage in AD reactors with high organic
contents.11 Therefore, it was reasonable to deduce that
denitrification was the main pathway for the NO3
−-N removal
pathway. Most of the time, NO2
−-N in all reactors was
maintained at a low level of nearly undetectable though the
Fe(III) and Fe(III)-AE10 groups attained relatively high
concentrations during days 20−25, with a maximum value of
3.9 and 2.9 mg/L being recorded on day 22, respectively
(Figure 2c).
The initial and final TN contents were measured to further
investigate the effects of iron sludge addition and intermittent
aeration on N removal (Figure 2d). The initial TN
concentration was 1197.7 mg/L in all groups. After digestion,
it decreased to 1161.7, 1028.8, 1015.7, 1012.1, and 999.1 mg/
L in the control, Fe(III), Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and
Fe(III)-AE15 groups, corresponding to a removal efficiency of
3.0, 14.1, 15.2, 15.5, and 16.5%, respectively. The decreased
TN by 3% in the control group might be attributed to the
small amount of Fe(III) in the inoculum derived from the
incubation process or the original fish feed. Fe(III)
supplementation and intermittent aeration greatly promoted
the removal of N during AD.

3.3. Changes of Iron. Only a proportion of the iron
content in solid iron sludge could be utilized by the IRBs, and
the supplemented iron sludge mixed in the fish sludge was
difficult to separate and tested. Therefore, the variations of
Fe(II) were monitored in this work instead of the total iron, as
the total iron concentrations could not reflect the changes of
iron induced by intermittent aeration and Feammox/DIR
reactions.33 It was reported that in the aerated solutions, the
half-life of dissolved Fe(II) was less than 5 min at
circumneutral pH.34 In this study, the system pH fluctuated
between 6.7 to 7.6 throughout the experiment in all reactors
(Figure S3). As shown in Figure 3, the concentration of Fe(II)
in the control group remained constant at about 670 ± 10 mg/
L throughout the experiment. A slight fluctuation of Fe(II)
between 1010.4 and 1186.5 mg/L during days 2−28 was
observed in the Fe(III) group. In sharp contrast, intermittent
aeration contributed to a much greater extent of Fe(II)
fluctuation. For example, the Fe(II) concentrations in the three
aerated reactors increased to about 1100 mg/L on day 2 due to
Feammox and/or DIR reactions; then, it decreased to 887.8,
784.3, and 754.5 mg/L on day 4 after being aerated for 5, 10,
and 15 min, respectively. Rapid Fe(II) oxidation occurred in
the reactors undergoing redox cycling, leading to the
regeneration of Fe(III). The variation of Fe(II) confirmed
the occurrence of the Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle induced by
intermittent aeration. Remarkably, the Fe(II) levels were
significantly different among the three reactors with different
aeration intensities (p < 0.05). The ranges of Fe(II) fluctuation
followed an order of Fe(III)-AE15 > Fe(III)-AE10 > Fe(III)-
AE5, confirming that a higher aeration intensity indeed
promoted the oxidation of Fe(II) to Fe(III). It was noticeable
that the amplitude of Fe(II) fluctuation became weaker with
time. On the one hand, the active (amorphous) Fe(III)
(hydr)oxide could be transformed into thermodynamically
more stable crystalline minerals (e.g., magnetite and Fe2O3)
with time,15 resulting in the decrease of microbial reducible
Fe(III). On the other hand, the Fe(II) could attach to the
surface of the Fe(III) compounds and be converted to iron
oxyhydroxide Fe(III), providing the nuclei for the formation of
secondary minerals and facilitating the uptake of aqueous
Fe(II), which further decreased the Fe(II) during redox
cycling.12
3.4. Microbial Metagenomic Analysis. To further reveal
the effects of iron sludge addition and its combination with
intermittent aeration on N removal, we annotated functional
genes of the microbial samples according to the Kyoto
Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database.
Specifically, functional genes involved in five N metabolism
processes were investigated, namely denitrification, dissim-
ilatory nitrate reduction, assimilatory nitrate reduction, N
fixation, and nitrification processes (Figure 4a). The
abundances of specific genes are indicated in Figure 4b. As
shown, the abundances of genes relative to nitrification were
very low, and anammox-related genes were not detected at all,
suggesting that neither nitrification nor Anammox was the
main pathway for ammonia conversion. In contrast, the total
abundances of denitrification-related genes were the highest
among the five N conversion processes studied, confirming
that denitrification played an important role in N removal from
the reactors. The abundances of denitrification-related genes
were generally higher in the Fe(III), Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-
AE10, and Fe(III)-AE15 groups with Fe(III) supplementation.
These results suggested that the supplementation of Fe(III)
must have induced certain reactions to convert NH4
+ into
NOx
−and subsequently drive the denitrification process. It is
worth mentioning that functional genes and proteins
associated with the Feammox process have not been identified
yet;11 therefore, the current study could not directly prove the
existence of Feammox-related genes. Despite this, the above
results could provide circumstantial evidence to support the
assumption that Fe(III)-induced Feammox coupled to
denitrification was the main N removal pathway during AD
of fish sludge. The abundances of genes relative to assimilatory
nitrate reduction (narB, nirA, and nasB) and N fixation (nif D/
H/K) were significantly lower compared with the genes
involved in dissimilatory nitrate reduction, indicating that
dissimilatory nitrate reduction was mainly responsible for the
regeneration of NH4
+-N in this study. As seen, the
supplementation of Fe(III) significantly decreased the
abundance of nirB, a key gene encoding NO2
−reductase
during dissimilatory nitrate reduction, which was beneficial to
the overall N removal performance.
To study the roles of different bacteria in N metabolism, we
further examined the sources of related functional genes.
Figure 4c,d displays the contributions of major taxonomic
groups to denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction
functions at the phylum and the genus levels, respectively. As
shown, the denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction
functions were mostly contributed by the same groups of
bacteria. The top four phyla contributing to denitrification
function in all reactors were Proteobacteria (34.2−40.5%),
Chloroflexi (23.9−28.1%), Bacteroidetes (10.6−13.4%), and
Planctomycetes (7.0−9.3%). Similarly, the above four phyla
contributed to 28.1−33.6, 27.7−33.2, 13.6−15.8, and 6.9−
8.9% of the overall dissimilatory nitrate reduction function,
respectively. On the genus level, unclassified_p__Chloroflexi,
unclassified_o__Bacteroidales, unclassified_f__Anaerolineaceae,
and unclassified_p__Betaproteobacteria were the main contrib-
utors to the denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction
functions.
The microbial communities in different experimental groups
were studied at the phylum level (Figure 5a) and genus level
(Figure 5b), respectively. As shown in Figure 5a, Chloroflexi
was the predominant phylum, accounting for 29.8−32.9% of
the overall microbial abundances, followed by Proteobacteria

The distributions of the genera are illustrated in Figure 5b.
Typical nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas, Nitrosococcus,
and Nitrospira,37 ammonia-oxidizing archaea such as Nitro-

Anammox bacteria including Kuenenia, Brocadia, Anammox-

exceeding 0.4 mg/L,6 ammonia-oxidizing archaea prefer an
acidic environment,40 and Anammox bacteria can be seriously
suppressed at high organic contents.30 In this study, the DO
concentrations in all reactors were not higher than 0.2 mg/L,
the pH levels were maintained at 6.7−7.6, and the TCOD
levels were 15−80 times higher than the inhibitory threshold
for Anammox bacteria, which were not suitable for the growth
of nitrifying bacteria, ammonia-oxidizing archaea, or Anammox
bacteria. Currently, the investigation on Feammox-related
microbes is still in the infancy, but studies have suggested that
IRBs (e.g., Longilinea, Bacteroides, Deltaproteobacteria, Acid-
obacteria, and Anaerolinea) are the primary functional bacteria
mediating Feammox.11,17,41 The relative abundances of IRBs
are shown in Figure 5c. As shown, the total abundance of IRBs
increased by 5.0−9.4% in the four Fe(III)-supplemented
reactors when compared with the control group, confirming
that the addition of iron sludge could enrich the IRBs, and this
was in agreement with the increased organic and NH4

removal efficiencies. Only one type of methanogen (Methano-

0.2, 2.6, and 13.8% in the Fe(III)-AE5, Fe(III)-AE10, and
Fe(III)-AE15 groups, respectively (Figure 5d). The abundan-

CH4 production performances.
3.5. Prospects. Iron sludge is a kind of solid waste
produced from the treatment of wastewater, the in situ
utilization of which is beneficial. This study demonstrated the
feasibility of SMFD in a single reactor treating fish sludge by
iron sludge addition and periodic air supply. Compared with
the conventional treatment processes (AD followed by
biological N removal), the SMFD system has the advantages
of a smaller footprint and much lower construction and
operational costs. The energy consumption of the complete
nitrification-denitrification process is about 4.6 kWh/kg N.11
While the energy consumption for aeration in the SMFD
system is negligible. The volumetric lower heating value of
CH4 is 35.8 MJ/m3.42 About 30% of the heat released from
CH4 combustion can be converted into electricity, and the
electricity production from CH4 is calculated to be 3.0 kWh/
m3. Although intermittent aeration showed a negative impact

on the CH4 yield, this was acceptable compared with the

conditions (5 min every 3 days), the electricity saved for N
removal was 44.7% higher than the decreased amount
recovered from CH4 production. Despite the merits of the
integrated system, the overall N removal efficiency was greatly
limited by the slow electron transfer between NH4
+-N and
Fe(III). To improve the overall N removal performance, future
research efforts should focus on further optimization of process
parameters (e.g., pH, temperature, C/N ratio, etc.) for
enhancing the activities of Feammox bacteria and acceleration
of interspecies electron transfer by adding redox-active
compounds or chelating agents.
Anaerobic decomposition of N-rich substrates such as fish
sludge, WAS, and animal manure often encounters elevated
concentrations of ammonia. Ammonia inhibition is one of the
most common causes of instability in industrial biogas plants.
The SMFD system provides a cost-effective alternative to
alleviate ammonia inhibition during AD. It is noteworthy that
Fe(III) is preferentially utilized in the DIR process over
ammonia oxidation. In this study, with the depletion of labile
organics, the removal of NH4
+-N became faster at the late stage
of methanogenesis, and a long retention time was required for
sufficient ammonia removal from the AD reactors treating fish
sludge. This phenomenon suggested that the SMFD system
might not be the most suitable for the treatment of substrates
rich in easily biodegradable organics. However, it has great
potential for the treatment of low C/N wastewater or
refractory organic wastewater with high NH4
+-N contents
such as digestates or pharmaceutical wastewater. The DIR
process has been proven to be effective for the anaerobic
degradation of refractory organic compounds. In addition,
intermittent aeration can facilitate the growth of facultative
bacteria, thereby promoting the hydrolysis of macromolecular
compounds. By coupling iron sludge addition with intermittent
aeration, the N in wastewater can be removed in situ through
Feammox and denitrification, and the organic C can be further
degraded and recovered as CH4.
